families.s: HSE offshore operator, owner, employer and worker duty guidance
families.t: accepted safety case, workforce consultation, safe operation, hydrocarbon release, structural and process integrity, wells, pipelines, emergency plans and cooperation
f: Operators and owners are responsible for controlling health and safety risks on offshore installations.
An accepted safety case is required where the applicable regime demands it.
Safety representatives should be consulted during preparation, revision or review of the safety case.
The installation should operate in accordance with the current safety-case arrangements.
Effective measures should prevent uncontrolled releases of flammable or explosive substances.
Structural, process-plant, temporary-refuge and equipment integrity should be maintained.
Well and pipeline integrity should be maintained throughout their lifecycle by the responsible dutyholders.
Emergency plans and cooperation among employers and other parties are required.
families.g: Offshore duty performance depends on accepted arrangements, workforce consultation, hydrocarbon containment, asset and well integrity, emergency readiness, employer cooperation, competence and assurance.

families.s: HSE offshore ageing, life-extension, corrosion and materials-integrity guidance
families.t: ageing processes, asset integrity, lifecycle, materials selection, coatings, inspection, corrosion threats, fatigue, management of change and decommissioning
f: Ageing and life extension are key offshore asset-integrity priorities.
Ageing risk should be managed through the remaining production period and into decommissioning.
Corrosion and material degradation can threaten pressure systems and major-accident containment.
Integrity management should cover design, operation, inspection, maintenance, change, life extension and decommissioning.
Materials and coatings should be selected for the actual environment and degradation mechanisms.
Risk-based inspection should identify, assess and follow up credible corrosion threats.
Fatigue, brittle failure, erosion and fabrication defects can require controls beyond corrosion management.
Audit, review, repair and anomaly records should demonstrate that integrity decisions remain justified.
families.g: Ageing and corrosion risk depends on design life, environment, materials and coatings, operating conditions, inspection quality, degradation rates, anomalies, repair, management of change and decommissioning.

families.t: inherently safe design, loading, weakness, deterioration, accidental damage, jack-up operations, inspection, analysis, repair and lifecycle management
f: Structural integrity is fundamental to offshore workforce safety.
Inherently safe design should reflect recognised good practice and credible loading conditions.
Integrity should be maintained through a management system of inspection, analysis and repair.
Structural failure can cause immediate total loss of an installation.
Failure mechanisms include overload, inherent weakness and fabrication defects.
Ageing deterioration and accidental or rare-event damage should be assessed.
Operator actions during jack-up jacking or preloading can create structural risk.
Inspection findings, analytical models, repairs and changes should be controlled throughout the lifecycle.
families.g: Structural risk depends on design and loading, foundation and environment, fabrication quality, ageing and fatigue, accidental damage, operational actions, inspection, analysis, repair and change control.

families.s: HSE offshore inspection, emergency-response and major-hazard assurance guidance
families.t: risk-based inspection, operator performance, emergency response, active fire protection, functional safety, aviation, marine operations, human factors and corrective action
f: HSE prioritises offshore inspection using installation and operator risk information.
Operator performance is assessed against published inspection criteria.
Emergency-response arrangements are a specific inspection topic.
Hydrocarbon active fire protection and functional safety are inspected as major-hazard controls.
Aviation, marine and helideck operations form part of offshore assurance.
Human factors, industrial hygiene, mechanical and electrical disciplines are included in the inspection framework.
Materials, corrosion, wells, structures and pipelines are subject to specialist review.
Findings should lead to tracked corrective actions, verification and management review.
families.g: Inspection and emergency assurance depend on installation risk, operator performance, barrier condition, response capability, specialist disciplines, findings, corrective action, verification and review.

families.s: HSE major-accident-hazard pipeline regulation and ALARP guidance
families.t: onshore and offshore pipelines, natural gas, hazardous substances, integrity, legislation, goal-setting duties, ALARP, standards and inspection
f: HSE regulates health, safety and integrity for applicable natural-gas and other major-hazard pipelines.
The scope includes pipelines in Great Britain, territorial waters and the UK continental shelf.
The Energy Division covers transmission and distribution networks, storage facilities and associated high-hazard sites.
Pipeline legislation is goal-setting and requires risks to be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.
Relevant recognised good practice is expected as a minimum benchmark.
Current good practice is generally expected for new pipelines and significant new situations.
Equivalent standards may be used where the dutyholder can demonstrate an equivalent safety level.
Regulatory assurance combines legislation, inspection, standards and evidence of integrity management.
families.g: Pipeline regulatory risk depends on pipeline type and substance, route and population, pressure and diameter, lifecycle stage, standards, integrity controls, inspection evidence and ALARP demonstration.
